title: Perceiving those reasons depends on grace-changed will affections
source_text: XX. Verum ut rationum istarum vim percipiamus, & ad illas mentem, ut decet, advertamus, quodammodo pendet a nostra voluntate. Etenim ut quisque est affectus, ita judicat. Ac cupiditates terrenae quae voluntatem nostram a coelestibus avertunt, mentem etiam obscurant, & distinent, ne se applicet iis quae cupiditatibus ejusmodi repugnant, aut vim penetret rationum quae nos ab iis abducere debent, quales sunt illae quibus veritates fidei comprobantur. Ac proinde ut fidem concipiamus, necesse est per Dei gratiam voluntatem nostram immutari, & novos affectus in ea excitari, ne quicquam impediat quominus animum, sicut convenit, applicemus ad ea quae fidem suadent meditanda & consideranda, & vim eorum ita percipiendam, ut eorum ponderi credamus, & fides animis nostris ingeneretur, non ex mero aliquo voluntatis imperio, sed quia omnibus expensis vera esse fidei mysteria judicamus, eo certissimis argumentis adducti, & motivis maxime momentosis impulsi. Quod tamen ut fiat requiritur bonus aliquis voluntatis motus, & pia quidem ejus affectio, quae quodammodo veritati aditum in mentem aperiat, ut ex dictis manifestum est.
pass_a_gloss: But that we may perceive the force of those reasons and turn the mind to them as is fitting somehow depends on our will. For as each is affected, so he judges. And earthly desires that turn our will from heavenly things also darken and hold back the mind, lest it apply itself to what resists such desires, or penetrate the force of the reasons that ought to lead us away from them — such as those by which faith's truths are proved. And therefore that we may conceive faith, it is necessary that by God's grace our will be changed and new affections stirred in it, lest anything hinder us from applying the mind, as is fitting, to meditating and considering what persuades faith, and so perceiving their force that we believe their weight, and faith be generated in our minds not from some mere empire of the will, but because all things weighed we judge faith's mysteries true, led by most certain arguments and driven by most weighty motives. Yet for this to happen some good motion of the will is required, and indeed a pious affection of it, which somehow opens an entrance for truth into the mind, as is clear from what has been said.
pass_b_english: Grasping faith's reasons somehow hangs on the will: as one is affected, so one judges.
Grace must change will-affections so the mind can weigh motives; faith rises from judged truth, not bare will-imperium — yet pious affection opens the door.
